analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states and cities that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 19, 2024, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal fund — $100 million a year for five years — to pay states, cities, and tribal governments that pass laws giving low-income tenants (incomes at or below 200% of the poverty line) a free lawyer in eviction cases and in cases where a housing subsidy is being taken away. Priority would go to governments that also limit no-fault evictions, require 30 days' notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance. It was introduced on the last day of the session's work and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never considered it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants (incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty line) facing eviction from their homes or loss of a housing subsidy would get a free lawyer paid for by federal grants, and the governments they live in would receive federal money to cover the cost. Most people facing eviction in court today have no attorney, and representation measurably improves the odds of staying housed.

how_it_helps.text: It creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund and authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029 for grants to states, local governments, and tribal governments that pass laws guaranteeing free, full legal representation to low-income tenants in eviction cases.
Covered tenants are those with incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty line, and covered cases include evictions from a primary residence and terminations of housing subsidies.

Federal grants would give priority to governments that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' written notice, run eviction diversion programs, provide emergency rental assistance, or recruit and train attorneys for tenants.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through $100 million per year in appropriations for fiscal years 2025 through 2029. Landlords in participating jurisdictions would bear slower, more contested eviction proceedings and, in prioritized jurisdictions, new limits on no-fault evictions and lease non-renewals.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $100 million per year in federal funds and attaches conditions encouraging states to restrict evictions, which landlord groups and fiscal conservatives would view as an expensive federal intrusion into landlord-tenant law that is traditionally set by states.

The grants are conditional: no money flows to a state or city unless it first enacts its own right-to-counsel law, so the bill by itself would not guarantee a lawyer to any tenant — it only subsidizes governments willing to act, which limits its reach in states that decline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: most tenants facing eviction go to court without a lawyer, and studies of existing right-to-counsel programs show represented tenants are far more likely to stay housed. The cost — $500 million over five years — is modest next to the public cost of homelessness. Its main design weakness is that the money only flows to governments that first pass their own right-to-counsel laws, so it rewards jurisdictions already inclined to act rather than creating a national guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the new Congress began.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 19, 2024, and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It attracted no cosponsors, giving it no visible support beyond its sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords facing potential eviction restrictions gained by the bill's death; tenants without counsel lost nothing they had but gained nothing either.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 19, 2024 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Landlord and real estate industry groups
against.what_they_did: Consistently oppose right-to-counsel and eviction-restriction measures at the state and federal level; no position on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever took shape; it died before any vote.

industries.note: Federal funding would go only to jurisdictions that guarantee lawyers for low-income tenants and would favor jurisdictions that restrict no-fault evictions and require 30 days' notice, making it harder and slower to remove nonpaying or at-fault tenants. The bill died, so nothing changed.

industries.industry: Legal aid organizations and tenant-side attorneys
industries.note: The bill would have funded training and recruitment of attorneys to represent tenants in eviction cases, a new revenue stream for legal services. Nothing was enacted.
